figures.caption: Figure 2: Harmonic Theory of target-seeking and avoidance. A: The density map of trajectories of an agent starting from the white circle and facing an attractive stimulus (green circle) for the first four harmonics is plotted. The nth harmonic has n fixed-bearing minima at ψ = 2kπ/n, k ∈ {1, . . . , n}, with respect to bearing to the target. This leads to a direct approach for the first harmonic and alignment (where both direct approach, ψ = 0, and direct escape, ψ = π, are possible) for the second harmonic. B and C: The agent’s trajectories result from the superposition of harmonics controlled by neuro-sensory parameters, W and σ. For small σ, the contribution of higher harmonics is weighted more strongly, leading to a spiral approach to the target (B). The attenuation of higher harmonics for large σ leads to a direct approach to the target and back-and-forth motion resulting from bifurcations between direct escape and direct approach, once the agent reaches the target (C). D: The density map of trajectories of the agent when facing a repulsive stimulus (red circle) for the first four harmonics is plotted. For repulsive interactions, the nth harmonic has n fixed-bearing minima at ψ = (2k + 1)π/n, k ∈ {1, . . . , n}, with respect to bearing to the target. This leads to direct escape for the first harmonic and perpendicular preferred headings (ψ = π/2 or 3π/2 at fixed bearing, which do not imply circular motion) for the second harmonic. E and F: For small σ, high contribution of higher harmonics degrades target-avoidance, induced by the first harmonic, leading to late turning away from the target (E). The attenuation of higher harmonics for large σ leads to direct escape from the target early on (F). Parameter values: veff0 = 1 and η = 0.1. In A to C, h = 1, and in D to F, h = −1. In A and D, σ = 0.1 and W = 0.903, and in other panels, W = 3π/5 and nmax = 1024. The deterministic dynamics (Dr = 0) is considered.

Figure 4: Binary escape problem in the Harmonic Theory. A: The decomposition of behavior into harmonic modes in the binary escape problem, where the agent faces two equal repulsive stimuli, reveals that the first harmonic is the fundamental mode leading to escape from average repulsive stimuli, while higher harmonics often lead to movement towards the repulsive stimuli, or a random-walk-like behavior for very high harmonics. B and C: The potential landscape when the agent is located along the symmetry axis and for two different values of angular separation of the targets, ∆, is presented. The attenuation of higher harmonics for large σ leads to a simplified potential landscape. Far away from the repulsive stimuli (small ∆ in B), the agent exhibits direct escape along the symmetry axis, ϕ = 3π/2. B(i) shows the potential landscape exhibiting a single minimum at ϕ = 3π/2, corresponding to direct escape. In B(ii), a colormap of 240 runs when the agent’s initial position corresponds to an angular separation, ∆init = 1.7, is presented. Closer to the stimuli, implying larger ∆init, the extremum at ϕ = π/2, corresponding to direct approach along the symmetry axis, becomes stable (C(i)). Colormap of 240 runs in C(ii) indicates bistability, where both direct escape and direct approach along the symmetry axis are possible. D: The stable heading directions along the symmetry axis for the first four harmonics, and the superposition of harmonics up to nmax = 512 is shown as a function of ∆. A subcritical bifurcation, above which the system becomes bistable, is observed (black line). E: For small σ, higher harmonics contribute more strongly, and the reported trajectories include motion towards the repulsive stimuli. F: A colormap of 240 runs in the bistable region (the same parameter values as in C(ii)) in the presence of noise is presented. By facilitating escape from approach states, noise improves avoidance behavior. Parameter values: In A, B(ii), C(ii), E, and F: veff0 = 1, h1 = h2 = −1, W = 3π/5, η = 5, and (other than A) nmax = 512. In B(i), C(i), and D: h1 = h2 = −1, W = 3π/5, nmax = 512. Dr is 0 in A, and it is shown in other panels (if applicable). In A snapshots show the results of 24 runs starting from random initial heading in the interval [0, π]. In other panels (if applicable), 240 runs starting from random initial heading in the interval [0, 2π] are used.

Figure 6: Collective motion in the Harmonic Theory. A: Snapshots of 80 agents as a function of time and for two different values of collision radius, rcoll, are plotted. For small or zero collision radius, agents form bidirectional columns (i). As the collision radius increases, spontaneous direction selection leads to unidirectional columns with an increased column width to avoid collisions (ii). B: Introducing collision avoidance leads to the formation of unidirectional columns. Global order (angular order parameter in i) and global nematic order (ii) are plotted as a function of collision radius, rcoll, and social attraction (the strength of stimuli), h. For medium values of h, high order is observed. While nematic order is always high in this region, indicating the formation of bidirectional columns, global order is high only for larger values of collision radius, indicating the formation of unidirectional columns due to collision avoidance. C: Introducing distance-dependence of stimuli leads to the formation of unidirectional columns. Global order (i) and global nematic order (ii) as a function of inverse characteristic length of stimuli, normalized by arena size (L/ξ), and the stimulus strength are plotted. For small L/ξ, the characteristic length of interaction is too high compared to the system size, and interactions are effectively all-to-all (independent of distance). In this regime, the alignment force in the effective Hamiltonian (even harmonics) is symmetric under reflection, and bidirectional columns are observed. When L/ξ increases (i.e., interaction range becomes smaller), the distance dependence of social attraction promotes the formation of unidirectional columns. Parameter values: N = 80, veff0 = 2, W = 0.9033, σ = 0.1. Here, up to the first nmax = 64 harmonics are superimposed. In A and B interactions are distance-independent at long range (attractive with strength h), and repulsive with strength hcoll = −10 below the collision radius, rcoll. In A, h = 0.05. In C, the amplitude of social stimuli is an exponential, h exp(−d/ξ), with characteristic length ξ, where d is the distance.

Figure 7: Collective motion resulting from only repulsion in the Harmonic Theory. A: Global order as a function of normalized inverse characteristic length of the stimuli, L/ξ, and its strength, h, is plotted. Here, the interactions are distance-dependent, according to an exponential, h exp(−d/ξ), with h < 0, leading to repulsive stimuli. Global order can reach a high value, indicating that collective motion in the Harmonic Theory can arise from repulsion alone. Collective motion exhibits a wide range of patterns, ranging from subgroup formation, where agents form aligned subgroups performing ballistic motion (B), band formation with group decomposition, where the population forms parallel bands, moving perpendicular to the common bearing of the agents along the band (C), or forming a single band with weak fission-fusion dynamics (D), collective motion with strong fission-fusion dynamics (E), and subgroup formation with rotational milling, where subgroups are located on vertices of a lattice, exhibiting unidirectional or bidirectional rotational milling (F). Parameter values: N = 80, veff0 = 2, W = 0.9033, σ = 1 (in A). Here, up to the first nmax = 32 harmonics are superimposed. Interactions are distance-dependent according to an exponential, h exp(−d/ξ), where d is the distance and ξ is the characteristic length.

Figure 8: Collective motion in the Harmonic Theory in a bounded space. A to C: The phase diagram of the collective motion in a bounded space (stadium) is plotted (A). For a small sensory kernel, σ, agents remain nearly stationary close to the walls, leading to a small distance to the walls and a small nearest-neighbor distance. As σ increases, for medium h, a milling phase, where agents exhibit stronger rotational motion, is observed. However, the rotational motion closely follows the boundary of space, such that angular momentum shows periodic peaks when agents approach curved boundaries where they turn in a coordinated fashion (see C for time series of normalized angular momentum and global order). For yet larger σ, agents form moving columns going back and forth along the stadium (B), leading to periodic peaks in global order (C). Increasing h, agents exhibit aggregates leading to a small nearest-neighbor distance. The aggregate can be stationary or move slowly, giving rise to lower and higher global order, depending on the values of h. For too large h and σ, the aggregate decomposes into subgroups, where the majority of agents exhibit ballistic motion. For too large h and medium σ, stationary column formation with high ordering and correlated longitudinal and transverse fluctuations along the columns or fission-fusion dynamics with the formation of networked corridors are observed. In this regime, agents naturally form networked corridors in space. D: D(i) and D(ii) show a snapshot of the collective motion pattern, where the population shows stationary networked corridor formation and intermittency between milling and column formation, respectively. Parameter values: N = 80, veff0 = 2, W = 0.9033, hcoll = −1, and Dr = 0. Interactions are distance-dependent, attractive according to an exponential with characteristic length ξ (ξ = 125 in the stadium and ξ = 250 in the circular arena). Short-range repulsion is included below distance rcoll (rcoll = 64 in A to C and rcoll = 16 in D). In A to C, agents move in a rectangular arena with length 1000 and width 200, where the two ends are semicircular (half-circle) with radius 100. In D, agents move in a circular arena with radius 500. Here, up to the first nmax = 64 harmonics are superimposed.
